title: R + AI Community Needs Survey: Tools, Trust, Reproducibility, and Real-World Workflows
text:
The R community is rapidly exploring new ways to use AI for programming, statistical analysis, reproducible research, and production workflows. To help understand where the community is today and tomorrow, R Consortium is conducting this short survey in advance of the R+AI 2026 event, which will be held the second week of November 2026.
Survey responses will help shape future R Consortium webinars, working groups, educational resources, and R+AI programming.
As a thank you for participating, respondents who choose to provide their email address will receive early access to the survey results and community analysis before they are presented publicly. We hope the findings will help R users better understand emerging trends, tools, and priorities across the R + AI ecosystem.
The survey takes approximately 7–10 minutes to complete, and respondents who share an email get early access to the results. Please join the survey, we really value your input!
Take the Survey

title: R+AI 2026 Workshops
text:
Tuesday, November 10, 2026
3:40 PM - 4:40 PM Eastern (1 hour)
Format: Live workshop



The R Validation Hub’s risk-based framework – evaluating R packages on purpose, maintenance practices, community usage, and testing – has become foundational for using R in regulated submissions. At the same time AI tooling has matured enough that some consider it is a plausible candidate for helping in some tasks such as assisting assessors in reviewing maintenance signals at scale, drafting or evaluating remediation tests, flagging changes across package versions.
AI also raises an issue in return: how should risk assessment treat packages or contributions that are themselves AI-generated or AI-assisted?
This workshop is designed to gather people with hands-on experience in R package validation, regulated environments, and applied AI tooling for a working discussion.
Where AI can realistically help within the existing framework
Where AI-assisted evaluation introduces new risks that would themselves need validation
What a minimal, practical pilot of AI- assisted risk assessment could look like
Session notes and points of consensus will be captured and used as the starting point for a community whitepaper
Topic: Evaluation, Observability, Responsible AI, and Governance






R Validation Hub Working Group; Strategic Platform Lead for Life Sciences at Appsilon

Ileana is the Strategic Platform Lead for Life Sciences at Appsilon, where she guides the direction of the platform’s team offering for the industry. She brings more than 8 years in pharma and biotech and over 14 years of using R. As Vice Chair of the R Validation Hub, she supports the responsible, risk-based use of open-source software in regulated settings. Ileana believes science and research deserve environments and infrastructure that match their needs for reproducibility, traceability and innovation, and that open-source solutions are a massive part of getting there. Above all, she is passionate about giving researchers tools they can trust, build on and enjoy using.
LinkedIn



Chair, R Validation Hub; Product Lead, Life Sciences, Domino Data Lab

Doug brings 10 years of Pharma and open source experience, with a focus on the human and process questions that steer clinical delivery. He Chairs the R Validation Hub as part of the R Consortium, which advocates for responsible risk-based adoption of open source tools, which invites new questions in the era of AI regarding how we express trust in software. Doug is also the Product Lead for Life Science at Domino, where he applies this philosophy of trust, reproducibility and traceability to deliver a rigorous platform for GxP workloads. Above all, Doug’s passionate about fostering open-source software that empowers people, be that through collaboration, decision-making, scientific rigor, reproducibility or even just to make analysis fun.

title: R+AI 2026 Workshops
section: From Lab to Production: Shipping R-Powered Drug Discovery Models as Apps on an Enterprise AI/Data Platform
text:
From Lab to Production: Shipping R-Powered Drug Discovery Models as Apps on an Enterprise AI/Data Platform



Date & Time
Wednesday, November 11, 2026
12:35 PM - 1:35 PM Eastern (1 hour)
Format: Live tutorial


Description
Most machine learning models built in R for drug discovery never leave the researcher’s laptop. This talk is a case study of taking R-based models from exploratory lab code to a governed, production AI application on an enterprise data platform.
At the center is the R pipeline: reproducible data preprocessing, molecular feature engineering, model training, and scoring, packaged to run reliably against enterprise data. I’ll show how this pipeline is version-controlled, containerized, and served behind a Streamlit frontend so scientists can query predictions without touching code.
I’ll also cover the realities of shipping AI in a regulated domain: secure deployment, private or managed models that keep proprietary chemistry in-house, production monitoring, and cost control at scale. Attendees will leave with a concrete blueprint for operationalizing R machine learning, plus the practices that make R pipelines reproducible, auditable, and trusted in a regulated environment.
Topic: Production AI and Industry Case Studies





Chanin Nantasenamat, PhD
Lead Developer Advocate, Snowflake

Chanin Nantasenamat, PhD is a Lead Developer Advocate at Snowflake, where he creates educational content on building data and AI applications with Streamlit and Snowflake. He recently co-developed the Coursera course “Fast Prototyping of GenAI Apps with Streamlit,” part of a DeepLearning.AI × Snowflake collaboration empowering developers to build GenAI applications. Chanin launched the social learning initiatives 30 Days of Streamlit and 30 Days of AI, which had helped introduced developers on building data and AI apps.
Before entering tech, Chanin was a full Professor of Bioinformatics, where he applied Python and R to computational drug discovery. He published extensively on machine learning research in this field, authoring 141 research articles, 21 review articles, and 6 book chapters. He has also presented at the R User Group at the Harvard Data Science Initiative.
Chanin is the creator of the Data Professor YouTube channel, with an audience of 220,000 subscribers. His 400+ videos (including dedicated playlists on R 101, R Data Science, and R Shiny) have earned over 10 million views. He has also created tutorials for the freeCodeCamp channel that amassed more than 2 million views. Together, his work bridges rigorous research, hands-on teaching, and a thriving open-source community.

title: Call for Proposals
section: R+AI 2026 Call for Proposals: Technical Areas
text:
R+AI 2026 Call for Proposals: Technical Areas
Foundations of Modern AI for R Users
Tutorials and primers that help R users understand today’s AI stack in practice: foundation models, embeddings, vector search, provider and model selection, cost and latency trade-offs, local versus hosted models, and how modern AI fits alongside classical machine learning in R.
LLM Engineering in R
Sessions on building reliable LLM workflows in R, including structured outputs, tool and function calling, retrieval, prompt and context design, batching, caching, file and image inputs, and hybrid R/Python patterns.
Agents, MCP, and Tool Ecosystems
Talks on agentic workflows in R: MCP servers and clients, multi-agent orchestration, skills, memory, tool registries, package-aware assistants, and hybrid architectures that keep R at the center of the workflow.
AI-Assisted R Development and Coding Workflows
How AI is changing R development: code generation, refactoring, debugging, documentation, test creation, review, migration, package maintenance, legacy-code modernization, and IDE-native assistance.
Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Multimodal AI in R
Not every AI workflow is an LLM. This track covers tabular ML, forecasting, causal ML, tidymodels, torch, geospatial deep learning, computer vision, multimodal pipelines, and other predictive workflows where R remains strong.
AI-Powered Data Products and Conversational Analytics
Building chat-enabled Shiny apps, analyst copilots, natural-language dashboards, reactive data interfaces, and human-in-the-loop tools that turn questions into auditable analysis and visual output.
Evaluation, Observability, Responsible AI, and Governance
How to evaluate AI systems in R, compare performance, cost, and latency, instrument applications, manage prompt and tool regressions, document behavior, and address privacy, reproducibility, bias, fairness, and regulatory expectations.
Production AI and Industry Case Studies
Frameworks, architectures, and case studies for shipping AI with R in real organizations: secure deployment, private or managed models, enterprise platforms, monitoring, cost control, procurement constraints, and lessons learned in healthcare, pharma, finance, marketing, manufacturing, research, and the public sector.

section: KEYNOTE ADDRESSES
text:
KEYNOTE ADDRESSES

Andrew Heiss, Ph.D., Assistant Professor of International Politics and Policy, Georgetown University in Qatar

Opening Keynote
Date & Time: November 10 at 8:00 AM, Eastern



Bio
Andrew Heiss’s research examines how international NGOs work in authoritarian countries. He received the 2016–2018 Emerging Scholar Dissertation Award from the International Society for Third Sector Research (ISTR). He also works in public administration and policy, nonprofit management, international relations, and comparative politics.
He teaches quantitative research methods and data science, program evaluation and causal inference, data visualization, economics, and science communication. He is a certified RStudio instructor and a Posit Academy mentor.



Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, Professor of the Practice at Duke University & Developer Educator at Posit, PBC

Closing Keynote
Date & Time: November 11 at 3:15 PM, Eastern



Bio
Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel is Professor of the Practice of Statistical Science and the Director of Undergraduate Studies in the Department of Statistical Science, as well as an affiliated faculty member in the Computational Media, Arts, and Cultures program at Duke University. Her work is dedicated to advancing innovation in statistics and data science pedagogy, focusing particularly on computing, reproducible research, student-centered learning, and open-source education. She emphasizes integrating computation into the undergraduate statistics curriculum, employing reproducible research methodologies, and analyzing real and complex datasets.

text:
The R Consortium and its working groups are dedicated to providing a harassment-free experience for participants at all of our events, whether they are held in person or virtually. R Consortium events are working conferences intended for professional networking and collaboration within the open source community. They exist to encourage the open exchange of ideas and expression and require an environment that recognizes the inherent worth of every person and group. While at R Consortium events or related ancillary or social events, any participants, including members, speakers, attendees, volunteers, sponsors, exhibitors, booth staff and anyone else, should not engage in harassment in any form.
This Code of Conduct may be revised at any time by The R Consortium and the terms are non-negotiable. Your registration for or attendance at any R Consortium event, whether it’s held in person or virtually, indicates your agreement to abide by this policy and its terms.


All event participants, whether they are attending an in-person event or a virtual event, are expected to behave in accordance with professional standards, with both this Code of Conduct as well as their respective employer’s policies governing appropriate workplace behavior and applicable laws.



Harassment will not be tolerated in any form, whether in person or virtually, including, but not limited to, harassment based on sex, gender, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, race, age, religion or any other status protected by laws in which the conference or program is being held. Harassment includes the use of abusive, offensive or degrading language, intimidation, stalking, harassing photography or recording, inappropriate physical contact, sexual imagery and unwelcome sexual advances or requests for sexual favors. Any report of harassment at one of our events, whether in person or virtual, will be addressed immediately. Participants asked to stop any harassing behavior are expected to comply immediately. Anyone who witnesses or is subjected to unacceptable behavior should notify a conference organizer at once.
Exhibitors should not use sexualized images, activities, or other material in their booths and must refrain from the use of sexualized clothing, uniforms, costumes, or otherwise creating a sexualized environment. Speakers should not use sexual language, images, or any language or images that would constitute harassment as defined above in their talks.
Individuals who participate (or plan to participate) in R Consortium events, whether its an in-person event or a virtual event, should conduct themselves at all times in a manner that comports with both the letter and spirit of this policy prohibiting harassment and abusive behavior, whether before, during or after the event. This includes statements made in social media postings, on-line publications, text messages, and all other forms of electronic communication.



If a participant engages in harassing behavior, whether in person or virtually, the conference organizers may take any action they deem appropriate depending on the circumstances, ranging from issuance of a warning to the offending individual to expulsion from the conference with no refund. The R Consortium reserves the right to exclude any participant found to be engaging in harassing behavior from participating in any further R Consortium events, working groups, trainings or other activities.
If a participant (or individual wishing to participate in an R Consortium event, in-person and/or virtual), through postings on social media or other online publications or another form of electronic communication, engages in conduct that violates this policy, whether before, during or after a R Consortium event, the R Consortium may take appropriate corrective action, which could include imposing a temporary or permanent ban on an individual’s participation in future R Consortium events, events, working groups, trainings or other activities.



If you are being harassed, notice that someone else is being harassed, or have any other concerns relating to harassment, please contact a member of the conference staff immediately. You are also encouraged to contact conduct@r-consortium.org.



Our staff has taken incident response training and responds to harassment reports quickly and thoroughly. As referenced above, if a participant engages in harassing behavior, whether in-person or virtually, the conference organizers may take any action they deem appropriate, ranging from issuance of a warning to the offending individual to expulsion from the conference with no refund, depending on the circumstances. The R Consortium reserves the right to exclude any participant found to be engaging in harassing behavior from participating in any further R Consortium events, working groups, trainings or other activities.
Conference staff will also provide support to victims, including, but not limited to:

Providing an Escort
Contacting Hotel/Venue Security or Local Law Enforcement
Briefing Key Event Staff For Response/Victim Assistance
And otherwise assisting those experiencing harassment to ensure that they feel safe for the duration of the conference.




If you are planning to attend an upcoming event, whether in-person or virtually and have concerns regarding another individual who may be present, please contact conduct@r-consortium.org. Precautions will be taken to ensure your comfort and safety, including, but not limited to providing an escort, prepping onsite event staff, keeping victim and harasser from attending the same talks/social events and providing onsite contact cell phone numbers for immediate contact.

title: R+AI 2026 Abstracts
section: From Statistical Models to Generative AI: Why Statistical Thinking Still Matters in the R+AI Era
text:
From Statistical Models to Generative AI: Why Statistical Thinking Still Matters in the R+AI Era
Date & Time: November 10 at 8:50 AM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: Evaluation, Observability, Responsible AI, and Governance
Co-Presenter: Sharanya Prasad, Senior Product Manager, Amazon Web Services


Abstract
Generative AI is rapidly changing how we work with data and write analytical code, including within the R ecosystem. Yet, as AI becomes increasingly capable of generating code, models, visualizations, and analytical narratives, the need for statistical thinking becomes more important—not less.
This talk explores how foundational statistical principles can guide the responsible and effective use of Generative AI in data analysis with R. Through practical examples, we will examine situations in which AI-generated analyses can produce plausible but misleading conclusions, including issues related to data quality, sampling, uncertainty, correlation and causation, model assumptions, bias, and interpretation.
The session will demonstrate how R can serve not merely as a coding environment, but as a tool for independently validating, reproducing, and critically evaluating AI-generated analytical results. We will also consider how the roles of statisticians and data analysts are evolving as AI increasingly participates in the analytical workflow.
The central message is simple: AI can generate code and analytical insights, but statistical thinking remains essential for determining whether those insights are valid, meaningful, and fit for decision-making.


Bio
Sahana Prasad brings more than 35 years of experience across academia, government and industry. She teaches and writes about data science and statistics using R, and has mentored researchers and trained faculty in applied analytics. Her books have been published by Springer Nature and Apress. She is also a recipient of the World Bank Statistical Capacity Building Award. Her work rests on one conviction: statistics earns its keep only when people can understand it, use it and trust it. She regularly publishes in Indian newspapers on varied topics.

To prompt or not to prompt? Why agentic AI is not the panacea.
Date & Time: November 10 at 9:30 AM, Eastern
Format: Lightning talk (15 minutes)
Topic: Agents, MCP, and Tool Ecosystems

Abstract
Agentic AI is everywhere in 2026, with 40% of enterprise apps expected to embed AI agents by year-end. Every new feature feels like reaching for an agent by default, because the tooling makes it so easy.
At the same time, Gartner forecasts 40% of agentic AI projects may be cancelled by 2027 due to unclear value and huge costs. This lightning talk cuts through the noise by discussing the following: what agents actually are, the levels of autonomy worth knowing, and when a simple prompt or rule beats an agent outright.

section: 50 lines of code to rebuild Claude Code in R
text:
50 lines of code to rebuild Claude Code in R
Date & Time: November 10 at 10:05 AM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: LLM Engineering in R

Abstract
Claude Code can feel like a complex piece of software, but its core ideas are surprisingly simple. In this talk, I’ll show how to rebuild its essential features in about 50 lines of R code. The result is a small coding agent that can read files, edit code, run commands, and ask for confirmation when needed.
We’ll walk through how it works and see how a simple loop and a few tools are enough to build a coding agent. Along the way, I’ll show how much ellmer handles for us, why it makes R a powerful environment for experimenting with AI agents, and how you can use these ideas to start building your own AI tools in R.

title: R+AI 2026 Abstracts
section: From Prompts to Pipelines: Building Auditable Human–AI Workflows for Evidence Synthesis in R
text:
From Prompts to Pipelines: Building Auditable Human–AI Workflows for Evidence Synthesis in R
Date & Time: November 10 at 10:45 AM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: LLM Engineering in R

Abstract
Large language models can accelerate evidence synthesis, but using them responsibly requires more than writing good prompts. This talk presents an R-based workflow for integrating LLMs into systematic review processes while preserving reproducibility, traceability, and human oversight. I will show how LLM-assisted screening, full-text assessment, structured data extraction, and normalization of concepts for narrative synthesis can be embedded in a reproducible targets pipeline, with prompt templates, structured JSON outputs, caching, validation checks, evidence quotation, and reviewer-facing quality-control reports. The talk focuses on practical lessons from building an auditable human-in-the-loop workflow and on design patterns that can help researchers move from isolated LLM calls toward more reliable and inspectable AI-assisted research pipelines.


Bio
Maciej is an R programmer and data scientist specializing in research design, reproducibility, and automation.
His work focuses on designing reproducible analytical workflows that combine methodological rigour with statistical programming and software engineering. He develops end-to-end R pipelines for clinical and social science studies, as well as evidence synthesis, using tools such as targets, Quarto, and renv.
His recent projects integrate large language models into systematic review workflows, with particular emphasis on screening assistance, structured evidence extraction, validation, human oversight, and methodological transparency.
He holds a master’s degree in psychology and has co-authored peer-reviewed scientific publications.
His professional interests lie at the intersection of research methodology, research software engineering, and philosophy of science, with a current focus on developing transparent, reproducible, and auditable human–AI research workflows.

title: R+AI 2026 Abstracts
section: Turtles All the Way Down: Recursive Language Models in R
text:
Turtles All the Way Down: Recursive Language Models in R
Date & Time: November 10 at 12:05 PM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: Agents, MCP, and Tool Ecosystems

Abstract
corteza is an LLM agent harness on CRAN. It answers the question, “What if we put an LLM in the R console instead of the command line?” In the literature, CodeAct and Recursive Language Models name this shape; in the market, Prime Agent.
The test case is ARC-AGI-3. With one prompt, corteza scored an official 98.6% on the public set with Claude Opus 5 and 100% with GPT-6 Astra, ahead of Prime Agent’s 95.5%. ARC’s adapter also scores 100% with Astra, but the metrics hide that corteza’s run was better. I’ll show the 894-helper workspace the model built mid-game.
The second recursion is the development loop. This experiment gave corteza a lessons store and thorough tracing of every R call, a dataset about the harness. saber gives an agent the same view of corteza’s code. Next, corteza analyzes data about its own harness and changes it.


Bio
Troy Hernandez is founder and CEO of cornball.ai, where he builds AI tooling in R. Since February 2026 he has published 25 CRAN packages and counting, including corteza, an LLM agent runtime that runs the model inside a live R session.
He earned his PhD in Statistics from the University of Illinois at Chicago in 2013, with a focus on applied machine learning, following an MS in Statistics and undergraduate degrees in mathematics and philosophy. Before founding cornball.ai he spent seven years at IBM as an Executive Architect and open source analytics evangelist, and worked as a data scientist at Civis Analytics, VivaKi, and Sears Holdings. He was a postdoctoral researcher at Tsinghua University and an AI advisor and mentor to NASA’s Frontier Development Lab. His research has appeared in PLoS ONE, the Journal of Computational Biology, and Transportation Research Record.
Troy has organized the Chicago R User Group since 2016, mentors early-career data scientists and developers, and shares his work through talks, tutorials, and posts at cornball.ai and troyhernandez.com.

section: Self-Documenting Shiny Applications with GitHub Actions, ChatGPT, and Playwright MCP
text:
Self-Documenting Shiny Applications with GitHub Actions, ChatGPT, and Playwright MCP

Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: Agents, MCP, and Tool Ecosystems

Abstract
When you build a Shiny application with Golem, you can structure it a lot like an R package. You can write tests with testthat, document your functions with roxygen2, and keep things like a README, NEWS file, and user guide alongside the code. That is great until the application starts changing faster than the documentation does.
In this talk, I’ll show how GitHub Actions, the ChatGPT API, and Playwright MCP can work together to handle a lot of that maintenance automatically. That includes updating documentation and tests, checking whether user workflows have changed, and creating new tutorial videos when they are actually needed. The goal is to spend less time chasing documentation updates and more time improving the application, while still keeping everything aligned with the code.

section: Ten Agents, 8GB of RAM, and Ten Dollars a Month
text:
Ten Agents, 8GB of RAM, and Ten Dollars a Month
Date & Time: November 10 at 1:25 PM, Eastern
Format: Lightning talk (15 minutes)
Topic: Agents, MCP, and Tool Ecosystems

Abstract
Ten AI agents run the back office of my consultancy. They track the market, draft content, triage my inbox and supervise each other, mostly while I sleep.
They run on a refurbished office desktop. 8GB of RAM, two hundred euros, five to ten dollars a month. The spec forbids Docker, Redis and any cloud database. The constraint did the design work.
Anyone can stand up agents now. Far fewer people talk about night forty, when the agents have been faithfully writing to a shared memory nobody is tidying and three quarters of it is repetition.
Three decisions determine whether a system like this still earns its keep a month in, and none of them are about the models. Where the memory lives. Who cleans it up. What establishes a fact before a model is allowed to interpret it.
No code on screen, no R required, no prior agent experience assumed. If you decide where AI goes in your organization, these are your decisions too.

title: R+AI 2026 Abstracts
section: Agentic Compactness: Measuring the Cost of AI-Generated Machine Learning Workflows in R
text:
Agentic Compactness: Measuring the Cost of AI-Generated Machine Learning Workflows in R
Date & Time: November 10 at 1:45 PM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: AI-Assisted R Development and Coding Workflows

Abstract
As AI coding agents increasingly build and repair machine learning workflows, the design of an R framework affects more than developer convenience. This talk introduces agentic compactness: the operational simplicity of a workflow measured through code length, framework calls, functions, objects, and package dependencies. Using matched classification and regression tasks, I compare funcml, mlr3, and tidymodels under shared learners, hyperparameters, data splits, validation, and scoring. The workflows achieve identical predictive performance but differ substantially in structural complexity, loading time, and memory use. A clinical genomics application demonstrates how funcml’s seven-verb interface supports an extended analysis. The talk concludes by showing how this benchmark can be extended to autonomous coding agents using first-run success, repair loops, and token consumption.


Bio
Imad El Badisy, PhD, is a health data scientist and computational methodologist at the Mohammed VI Center for Research and Innovation (CM6RI), Rabat, Morocco.
He builds open-source software for machine learning and computational biostatistics, turning advanced statistical methods into reliable tools that researchers can use. He holds a PhD from Aix-Marseille University (SESSTIM) on missing data and machine learning for survival analysis.
His research covers scientific machine learning, survival analysis, missing data imputation, and agentic data science: LLM-based agents that plan and run statistical workflows, and software designed so these agents can use it correctly, reproducibly, and safely. He maintains several R packages on CRAN, including funcml.

title: R+AI 2026 Abstracts
section: Utilizing Reproducible Agents in RStudio - A Researcher’s Toolkit
text:
Utilizing Reproducible Agents in RStudio - A Researcher’s Toolkit
Date & Time: November 10 at 3:00 PM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: Agents, MCP, and Tool Ecosystems

Abstract
ClaudeR is an R package and MCP server that connects AI agents to a live RStudio session.
The agent can code alongside you, act autonomously, guide you as you learn, edit select portions, annotate data, or check code claims against a manuscript—to name a few features. Every line it runs is logged and associated to the agent that ran it, and checkpoints make any step the agent takes reversible. Several agents from different sources (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, etc.) can share one session and coordinate through a consensus gate, or independent agents can work silo’d in parallel. Whatever your workflow is, the goal of this package is to accommodate it. This talk covers the architecture, how to use it, some example workflows, and what building it taught me about working with agents.


Bio
Nykko Vitali is a PhD student in the Psychology Department at Harvard University. Nykko’s research focuses on decision making under uncertainty in environments where LLMs may be present. He also examines the behaviors, both good and bad, that have seeped into models through pre- and post-training. Nykko built ClaudeR shortly after Anthropic released the Model Context Protocol (MCP), to explore agentic coding within a controlled harness. A year and a half later, the package supports auditable autonomous coding workflows, multi-agent coordination, manuscript reproducibility checks, and data annotation, among other tools for researchers. It now works with Python and Positron as well as R and RStudio, and has 350 GitHub stars. The goal throughout has been to let any MCP-capable LLM work inside RStudio while keeping an auditable script of what was done and when.

section: Enterprise AI Governance and Secure Grounding: Privacy, Zero Trust, and Observability in Agentic AI Systems
text:
Enterprise AI Governance and Secure Grounding: Privacy, Zero Trust, and Observability in Agentic AI Systems
Date & Time: November 11 at 8:00 AM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: Evaluation, Observability, Responsible AI, and Governance

Abstract
Deploying production-grade Copilot and agentic systems requires moving beyond basic prompt engineering to tackle complex challenges in data privacy, access control, and system observability. When AI agents dynamically query enterprise data stores and invoke external tools, traditional security boundaries quickly break down.
This session explores proven architectural patterns for enforcing Zero Trust security, privacy-preserving retrieval, and robust observability across enterprise AI platforms. Attendees will discover how to implement secure grounding layers that prevent data leakage and ensure granular access control during vector search and context retrieval. We will also examine strategies for continuous evaluation, tracking prompt and tool regressions, and monitoring system latency and performance at scale.
Whether integrated with Python microservices, R-based analytics platforms, or hybrid enterprise architectures, attendees will gain actionable frameworks to build, deploy, and govern secure, transparent, and resilient AI systems in production.


Bio
Karthik Chandrasekaran is a Principal Software Engineering Manager at Microsoft, where he leads engineering strategy and intelligent agent query-matching platforms for Microsoft 365 Copilot. His technical leadership focuses on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), vector search infrastructure, cloud-native architecture, and secure identity authentication frameworks.
Prior to Microsoft, Karthik held senior engineering leadership roles at Apple, Capital One, and PayPal, directing core identity systems, security infrastructure, and large-scale distributed platforms. An IEEE Senior Member, he actively contributes to the broader research and technical community through peer reviewing and program committee service for international conferences, including ICITCE, ICETICS, ISCI, and ICCA. R-Native Private AI for Sensitive Data: Secure Analysis and Code Modernization

Topic: AI-Powered Data Products and Conversational Analytics
Co-Presenter: Andey Nunes-Brewster, Data Interoperability Coordinator, Oregon Health Authority


Abstract
Almost every AI product assumes data can travel to the model. In public health and other regulated environments, that assumption breaks down. In this joint session with the Oregon Health Authority, we present a different model: bring AI into the analyst’s R environment rather than sending sensitive data out. Using PolyKode Assistance as the implementation, we show private AI integrated directly into the R IDE, supporting exploratory analysis, code generation, Shiny development, and modernization of legacy analytical code, while prompts, data, and outputs stay in the controlled environment. Attendees leave with a view of how to introduce AI into existing R workflows without abandoning the tools and controls they already rely on.

text:
Standardizing Molecular Diagnostic Metadata: An Automated Workflow Mapping FDA-Cleared NAAT Assays to Pathogen Taxonomy
Date & Time: November 11 at 10:15 AM, Eastern

Abstract
The primary objective of the IVD microbial NAAT registry workflow was to bridge the gap between unstructured FDA regulatory labels and validated taxonomic names. Developing this resource required synthesizing expertise across three distinct layers: (i) clinical diagnostics, (ii) pathogen nomenclature, and (iii) bioinformatic search patterns. title: R+AI 2026 Abstracts
section: Two Languages, One Conversation: An LLM-Powered R Shiny App served by a Python API
text:
Two Languages, One Conversation: An LLM-Powered R Shiny App served by a Python API
Date & Time: November 11 at 10:35 AM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: AI-Powered Data Products and Conversational Analytics

Abstract
At Ketchbrook Analytics, we’ve built a financial analysis dashboard that allows users to “Chat” with their data in R Shiny. The LLM agent behind it is built in Python. They meet in exactly one place: a streaming API endpoint.
On the Python side, a custom agent explores a curated data catalog, writes SQL, and even reads its own errors and retries.
On the R side, Shiny consumes the API response stream, using ExtendedTask and {future} so the app stays responsive while the model thinks. The user receives a neat data table, a summary analysis, and a custom chart that’s relevant to their prompt.
We’ll cover the “gotchas” we ran into, including how we handled streaming responses with {httr2}, efficiently served custom charts, and cut input costs by 59% through clever caching. The audience will leave with valuable tips and tricks for building an LLM-powered Shiny app.


Bio

He holds a Bachelor’s Degree in Accounting and Mathematics from Stonehill College, and a Master’s Degree in Business Intelligence & Analytics from Saint Joseph’s University. He is highly versed in the R, Python, and SQL programming languages, and holds a certification from RStudio (now Posit) in Data Science Education.

text:
From Experimentation to Trusted Production: A Practical Framework for R+AI in Regulated Industries
Date & Time: November 11 at 2:35 PM, Eastern
Format: Talk (35 minutes)
Topic: Production AI and Industry Case Studies
Co-Presenter: Siddharth Maheshwari, Senior Manager, Data & AI Solutions, ProCogia


Abstract
How do you move an R+AI workflow from a successful experiment into something a regulated organization can actually trust and operate in production? This talk presents a practical, reusable framework for preserving traceability, governance, reproducibility, and control as AI moves into higher-consequence workflows. We will use a deployment spectrum, from public AI services and enterprise APIs through private cloud, on-premises, and air-gapped environments, to show the trade-offs across control, speed, complexity, and cost. The goal is not maximum sovereignty, but choosing the level of control that matches the workload’s risk, value, and scale. Drawing on lessons from regulated analytics modernization and real production workflows, we will show how model selection, evaluation, observability, guardrails, validation, and human oversight fit together in practice. Attendees will leave with a reusable framework and readiness checklist for deciding what to control, validate, monitor, and govern before scaling R+AI.


Bio
Nammn Joshii is Director, AI Innovation and Delivery at ProCogia, where he leads enterprise data and AI transformation, strategic client engagements, and consulting delivery. He advises executives on translating AI, data, and technology strategy into scalable operating models and production-ready solutions that improve performance, reduce costs, and accelerate growth. With 13+ years of experience across technology and transformation, Nammn combines strategic perspective with hands-on delivery experience to help organizations navigate complex, technology-led change and move AI from experimentation into trusted enterprise use.

Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel is Professor of the Practice of Statistical Science and the Director of Undergraduate Studies in the Department of Statistical Science, as well as an affiliated faculty member in the Computational Media, Arts, and Cultures program at Duke University. Her work is dedicated to advancing innovation in statistics and data science pedagogy, focusing particularly on computing, reproducible research, student-centered learning, and open-source education.
